title: Should You Give Consequences Privately?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin walks through the appeal of using discreet hand signals to give consequences privately -- quiet, quick, respectful -- before systematically arguing the approach fails in practice for four concrete reasons: misbehaving students often aren't looking at the teacher and require the teacher to reposition directly in front of them; hand signals are frequently misread, especially by younger students; multiple nearby students often can't tell who's being targeted; and even when understood, silent signals lack the clarity and reassurance of a verbal statement. He directly rebuts the common counterargument that public consequences humiliate students, calling the concern -- which he attributes largely to uninformed administrators -- unfounded as long as the teacher doesn't berate or raise their voice, arguing that simply stating a broken rule and its consequence is truthful, not degrading. He closes by pointing out that misbehavior itself is rarely truly private in a room full of students who can see and hear it regardless, so attempting to conceal the consequence delivery doesn't actually protect the student from visibility.
points: Discreet hand-signal consequences fail in practice: students often aren't looking at you, signals get misread, and nearby students can't tell who's being targeted.
Even when understood, a silent signal lacks the clarity and reassurance that comes from simply verbalizing the rule and consequence.
Rebuts the claim that public consequences are humiliating -- calmly stating a broken rule and consequence is truthful, not degrading, as long as it's not delivered with berating or raised voice.
Misbehavior is rarely actually private in a classroom full of witnesses, so trying to conceal the consequence doesn't shield the student from visibility anyway.
quotes: A student misbehaves and you give them a hand signal letting them know which rule was broken and the consequence. The benefits are:

When a student is misbehaving, it’s often hard to get their attention. If you limit yourself to a hand signal, then you’ll have to position yourself—often directly in front of them—for them to notice you.
No matter how demonstrative you are, hand signals can be misinterpreted. In fact, they often prompt students to ask you to explain. The younger the students, the more this is the case.

Even if you have the attention of the rule-breaker and they understand the signal you give them, it’s human nature to want to be told. Verbalizing provides clarity and assurance. It’s why NFL referees have microphones.
Of course, you should never berate, raise your voice, or try to humiliate. But simply informing a student of what rule they broke and the consequence isn’t humiliation. It’s the truth.
You can’t hide it anyway. Even if you do try to use a non-verbal signal, your students can see the misbehavior. They can hear the disruption. Believing otherwise is silly.
